title: Project: A Multi-Agent Workflow with Human-in-the-Loop Checkpoints
summary: Build a production-style multi-agent workflow in LangGraph where a supervisor routes work to specialist agents, pauses at human approval gates before high-risk actions, and recovers gracefully from errors. You'll wire up shared state, conditional routing, interrupts with checkpointers, and resumable execution.
objectives: Design a supervised multi-agent topology with a router/supervisor and specialist worker agents in LangGraph
Model shared graph state and conditional edges to coordinate a multi-step business task
Implement human-in-the-loop approval gates using interrupts and a persistent checkpointer
Add error-recovery patterns (retries, fallbacks, and escalation to a human) for robust execution
Resume a paused graph from a saved checkpoint and feed in human decisions
Evaluate when to use human checkpoints versus full autonomy in production

quiz.q: What two LangGraph features together enable human-in-the-loop checkpoints?
options: LLM routing and tool calling
A checkpointer and an interrupt (e.g., interrupt_before)
Streaming and async nodes
Subgraphs and reducers
quiz.why: A checkpointer persists state per thread_id so the run can be paused and resumed, and interrupt_before/after halts execution to return control for human review.

quiz.q: Why is `Annotated[list, operator.add]` used for the errors field in state?
options: It encrypts the error messages
It limits the list to one item
It acts as a reducer so concurrent node writes append instead of overwrite
It converts errors to strings automatically
quiz.why: Reducers tell LangGraph how to merge state updates; operator.add appends lists so multiple nodes can record errors without clobbering each other.

quiz.q: After a graph pauses at an interrupt, how do you resume it with a human decision?
options: Restart the whole graph from scratch
Call update_state with the decision, then invoke with None and the same config
Delete the checkpoint and rebuild the graph
Call get_state repeatedly until it continues
quiz.why: You write the human's decision into state via update_state, then invoke with None on the same thread_id config so execution continues from the saved checkpoint.

quiz.q: Which actions are the best candidates for a human approval gate?
options: Every single node for maximum safety
Read-only data retrieval steps
Irreversible or high-risk actions like issuing a refund
LLM routing decisions
quiz.why: Gating should target irreversible or high-risk actions; over-gating reversible or low-risk steps destroys throughput without adding meaningful safety.

quiz.q: Why should MemorySaver be replaced in production?
options: It is slower than all alternatives
It does not support interrupts
Its state is in-memory and lost on restart, so use a durable saver like SqliteSaver or PostgresSaver
It cannot store TypedDict state
quiz.why: MemorySaver keeps state in memory, which is lost on process restart; durable checkpointers persist state so long-running, human-gated workflows survive restarts.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what is the role of the supervisor in this architecture?
quiz.answer: The supervisor inspects the shared state and decides which specialist agent runs next, looping until the task is complete.
quiz.why: The supervisor pattern centralizes routing: each worker returns to the supervisor, which reads state and chooses the next node or ends the run.

body_markdown:
## Project Overview

In this project you'll build a **supervised team of agents** that processes a multi-step business task: drafting and sending a customer refund decision. The workflow includes specialist agents, **approval gates** where a human must sign off before irreversible actions, and **error recovery** so transient failures don't crash the run.

The scenario: a customer submits a refund request. The system must (1) gather order data, (2) analyze policy eligibility, (3) draft a customer email, (4) **pause for human approval** before issuing the refund, then (5) execute and confirm.

## The Architecture

We use a **supervisor pattern**: a central supervisor node inspects the shared state and routes to the right worker. Workers are specialist agents:

- **Retriever** — fetches order and customer history.
- **PolicyAnalyst** — decides eligibility against refund rules.
- **Drafter** — writes the customer-facing message.
- **Executor** — issues the refund (the irreversible action, gated by a human).

The supervisor reads state, picks the next worker, and the graph loops back to the supervisor after each worker finishes until the task is `done`.

## Shared State

All agents read and write a single typed state object. Keep it explicit:

```python
from typing import TypedDict, Literal, Annotated
import operator

class RefundState(TypedDict):
    request: str
    order: dict | None
    eligibility: str | None        # "approved" | "denied" | "unclear"
    draft_email: str | None
    human_decision: str | None     # "approve" | "reject" | "edit"
    status: str                    # routing signal
    errors: Annotated[list, operator.add]
    next: str
```

Using `Annotated[list, operator.add]` lets multiple nodes append to `errors` without clobbering each other — this is how LangGraph reducers merge concurrent writes.

## Building the Supervisor

The supervisor is a function (or small LLM call) that returns the name of the next node. Keep routing deterministic where you can — LLM routing is powerful but harder to test.

```python
def supervisor(state: RefundState) -> dict:
    if state.get("order") is None:
        return {"next": "retriever"}
    if state.get("eligibility") is None:
        return {"next": "policy_analyst"}
    if state.get("draft_email") is None:
        return {"next": "drafter"}
    if state.get("human_decision") is None:
        return {"next": "approval_gate"}
    if state["human_decision"] == "approve":
        return {"next": "executor"}
    return {"next": "END"}
```

## Wiring the Graph

```python
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, END
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver

builder = StateGraph(RefundState)
builder.add_node("supervisor", supervisor)
builder.add_node("retriever", retriever)
builder.add_node("policy_analyst", policy_analyst)
builder.add_node("drafter", drafter)
builder.add_node("approval_gate", approval_gate)
builder.add_node("executor", executor)

builder.set_entry_point("supervisor")

def route(state): return state["next"] if state["next"] != "END" else END

builder.add_conditional_edges("supervisor", route)
for worker in ["retriever", "policy_analyst", "drafter", "executor"]:
    builder.add_edge(worker, "supervisor")

# Compile with a checkpointer and an interrupt BEFORE the gate
graph = builder.compile(
    checkpointer=MemorySaver(),
    interrupt_before=["approval_gate"],
)
```

## Human-in-the-Loop Checkpoints

Two things make HITL work in LangGraph:

1. **A checkpointer** (e.g., `MemorySaver`, or `SqliteSaver`/`PostgresSaver` in production) that persists state after every step, keyed by a `thread_id`.
2. **An interrupt** — `interrupt_before=["approval_gate"]` halts execution *before* the node runs, returning control to your application.

Run until the interrupt:

```python
config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "refund-123"}}
result = graph.invoke({"request": "...", "status": "new", "errors": []}, config)
# Execution pauses; inspect the draft
state = graph.get_state(config)
print(state.values["draft_email"])
```

A human reviews the draft and eligibility. To resume, update the state with their decision and invoke with `None`:

```python
graph.update_state(config, {"human_decision": "approve"})
final = graph.invoke(None, config)   # continues from the checkpoint
```

If the human edits the draft, write both the edit and the decision before resuming. The graph picks up exactly where it paused — no recomputation of earlier steps.

## Error Recovery

Production agents fail: APIs time out, the LLM returns malformed JSON, a tool 500s. Layer your defenses:

- **Retries with backoff** inside a node for transient errors.
- **Fallbacks**: if `policy_analyst` is unsure, route to a human instead of guessing.
- **Escalation**: append to `state['errors']`; the supervisor can route to an `approval_gate` or a `human_escalation` node when errors accumulate.

```python
def policy_analyst(state):
    try:
        result = call_llm_policy(state["order"])
        return {"eligibility": result}
    except Exception as e:
        return {"eligibility": "unclear", "errors": [str(e)]}
```

Because the checkpointer saves state after each node, a crash mid-run can be resumed from the last good checkpoint rather than restarted.

## Putting It Together — Run Loop

A real app exposes two endpoints: **start** (invoke fresh) and **resume** (after human input). Store `thread_id` so the human's later approval maps back to the right paused run. The same pattern scales to long-running tasks that wait hours or days for a human.

## Production Tips

- Use a durable checkpointer (`SqliteSaver`/`PostgresSaver`), not `MemorySaver`, so state survives restarts.
- Gate only **irreversible or high-risk** actions — over-gating destroys throughput.
- Log every state transition for auditability.
- Make routing testable: prefer deterministic supervisor logic, reserve LLM routing for genuinely ambiguous decisions.

slides.narration: Welcome. In this project lesson we'll build a supervised team of agents that handle a real multi-step business task — processing a customer refund — with human approval gates and error recovery baked in. slides.title: The Scenario & Architecture
bullets: Task: decide and issue a customer refund across 5 steps
Supervisor routes work to specialist agents
Workers: Retriever, PolicyAnalyst, Drafter, Executor
Executor is gated — humans approve before money moves
slides.narration: Our scenario is a refund request. A central supervisor inspects shared state and decides which specialist runs next. The Retriever pulls order data, the PolicyAnalyst checks eligibility, the Drafter writes the customer email, and the Executor issues the refund. That last step is irreversible, so we'll require a human to approve before it runs.

slides.title: Shared State Design
bullets: One typed state object read and written by all nodes
Track order, eligibility, draft, human_decision, status
Use reducers for fields written concurrently
Explicit state makes routing and testing easy
slides.code:
class RefundState(TypedDict):
    order: dict | None
    eligibility: str | None
    draft_email: str | None
    human_decision: str | None
    errors: Annotated[list, operator.add]
    next: str
slides.narration: Everything coordinates through one typed state object. Notice the errors field uses an annotated reducer with operator.add — that lets multiple nodes append errors without overwriting each other. Keeping state explicit makes your supervisor logic deterministic and your graph far easier to test and debug.

slides.title: The Supervisor Pattern
bullets: Supervisor returns the name of the next node
Loop: supervisor -> worker -> supervisor
Prefer deterministic routing; reserve LLM routing for ambiguity
Clear stop condition routes to END
slides.narration: The supervisor is just a function that looks at state and names the next worker. After each worker finishes, control returns to the supervisor, which decides what's next until the task is done. Wherever possible keep this logic deterministic — it's much easier to test than an LLM making routing calls every step.

slides.title: Wiring the Graph
bullets: add_node for supervisor and each worker
conditional_edges from supervisor based on state['next']
Every worker edges back to the supervisor
Compile with checkpointer + interrupt_before
slides.narration: We add every node, then conditional edges from the supervisor that route on the next field, and a plain edge from each worker back to the supervisor. The key line is compile: we attach a checkpointer and tell LangGraph to interrupt before the approval gate. Those two pieces are what enable human-in-the-loop.

slides.title: Human-in-the-Loop Checkpoints
bullets: Checkpointer persists state per thread_id after every step
interrupt_before halts execution and returns control
Inspect paused state with get_state
Resume by updating state and invoking with None
slides.code:
config = {'configurable': {'thread_id': 'refund-123'}}
graph.invoke(inputs, config)        # pauses
graph.update_state(config, {'human_decision': 'approve'})
graph.invoke(None, config)          # resumes
slides.narration: Here's the magic. The checkpointer saves state after every node, keyed by a thread id. When the graph hits the interrupt, it stops and hands control back to your app. You inspect the draft, a human decides, you write their decision into state with update_state, then invoke with None to resume exactly where it paused — no recomputation of earlier steps.

slides.title: Error Recovery Patterns
bullets: Retries with backoff for transient failures
Fallbacks: route to a human when an agent is unsure
Escalation: accumulate errors, then gate or hand off
Checkpoints let you resume after a crash
slides.narration: Production agents fail, so layer defenses. Retry transient errors inside the node, fall back to a human when an agent can't decide confidently, and escalate when errors pile up. And because state is checkpointed after each node, a crash mid-run can resume from the last good checkpoint instead of starting over.

slides.title: Production Tips
bullets: Use durable checkpointers: SqliteSaver / PostgresSaver
Gate only irreversible or high-risk actions
Log every state transition for audit trails
Map thread_id to user so resume routes correctly
slides.narration: To take this to production: swap MemorySaver for a durable Sqlite or Postgres checkpointer so state survives restarts and long waits. Only gate the truly risky actions — over-gating kills throughput. Log every transition for auditability, and store the thread id so a human's approval, even days later, resumes the right run. That's a robust, supervised, human-in-the-loop agent system.
